title: Testing motion sensors, monitoring recovery, and exploring views on smart knee replacements in people having a total knee replacement
official: Sensor validation, recovery tracking, and acceptability of smart implantable knee devices in patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty
summary:
Background and study aims
Total knee replacement (TKR) is a very common operation. Most patients recover well after the operation; however, some may experience problems such as joint infection or stiffness. It is important for clinicians to identify these problems as early as possible.
Sensors could help patients and clinicians monitor how the knee is recovering and identify changes that may need further investigation. Knee sensors are small electronic devices that can measure how the knee moves during everyday activities and exercise.
A new knee sensor has been developed at the University of Leeds. In the future, this sensor may be placed inside knee replacement implants. These are known as “smart knee implants”.
The first aim of this study is to find out how accurately the sensor measures knee movement when it is worn on the outside of the body.
The second aim is to understand how these measurements change as patients recover from their knee replacement operation.
The third aim is to find out what patients think about smart knee implants through interviews.
For this study, the sensor will not be implanted inside participants’ knees. It will only be worn on the outside of the body.

Who can participate?  
Patients aged 18 years or over who are waiting to have a total knee replacement operation

What does the study involve?  
Participants will attend three sessions at the gait analysis laboratory: one before their knee replacement operation and two during their recovery.
At the first session, participants will complete a consent form.
At each session, we will ask participants to wear comfortable sports-style clothing, such as shorts and trainers. We will then ask them to complete two short questionnaires. We will collect some basic information and measurements, such as their age, gender, height, weight and leg length. We will then attach small reflective markers and sensors to their legs. These will measure how their knees and legs move.
Participants will complete simple activities such as bending their knee, walking, using stairs, standing up from a chair and doing a squat. We may also ask them to complete some additional activities, depending on how they are feeling and what we need for the study. Participants can take breaks and stop any activity at any time.
At the end of each session, we will remove the markers and sensors.
Participants can also choose to take part in two optional interviews, one before and one after their knee replacement operation. During the interviews, a researcher will ask about their views on smart knee implants.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may not benefit directly from taking part in this study. However, the study may help us understand how this new sensor could be used to monitor recovery after total knee replacement. Participants who take part in the optional interviews will also have the opportunity to share their views and experiences from their operation.
At the end of the study, we will send participants a summary of the results. This will be available in standard, easy read and large print formats.
We do not expect any major risks from taking part. Some of the physical activities, such as walking or using stairs, may involve a small risk of tripping or falling. We will take steps to reduce these risks and will only ask participants to complete activities that are safe for them.
Taking part in the study will not affect participants' usual care.

Where is the study run from?  
Leeds Institute of Rheumatic and Musculoskeletal Medicine (LIRMM) (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
January 2027 to March 2028

Who is funding the study?  
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) HealthTech Research Centre in Accelerated Surgical Care (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Davide Ottaviani, dkgl0667@leeds.ac.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. 18 years of age or older
2. Undergoing primary unilateral or bilateral TKA
3. Able to attend their first data collection session within three months before their TKA operation
Exclusion criteria:
1. Unable to walk and climb stairs independently or with minimal assistance, including the use of walking aids such as walking sticks or crutches
2. Unable to transition from sitting to standing and from standing to sitting unaided, as well as to transition from getting up to lying down on a physiotherapy bed (and vice versa) unaided
3. Unable to perform basic lower limb rehabilitation exercises unaided or with minimal assistance
4. Pre-existing neurological or orthopaedic conditions, or any other pathologies that could impair the activities listed above
5. Undergoing partial knee replacement
6. Pregnant
7. Have any implantable electronic medical device (e.g., cardiac implantable electronic devices, cochlear implants, neural stimulators, infusion pumps, programmable hydrocephalus shunts)
8. Allergic to adhesives (e.g., sticky tape or plasters)
9. Not willing to wear appropriate clothing for the study sessions (sports clothing)
10. Have an active knee infection
11. Have an active cancer
12. Unable to provide informed consent
13. Have limited English language proficiency
